# Gaussian Splatting Deformation
Also called: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting, Time-varying Gaussian Splatting
## Overview
Gaussian Splatting Deformation extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by modeling time-dependent geometric and appearance parameters, solving the problem of reconstructing and rendering moving subjects from multi-view video . It sets itself apart from sibling methods by decomposing the 4D representation into a static canonical set of Gaussians and a deformation function that predicts their state at any time $t$, distinguishing it from [Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields](17161-space-time-neural-irradiance-fields.md) which use neural fields, [Dynamic NeRF](21867-dynamic-nerf.md) which uses volumetric ray marching, and [Neural Scene Flow Fields (NSFF)](21905-neural-scene-flow-fields-nsff.md) which predicts explicit scene flow vectors .
## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of canonical space deformation. A static set of 3D Gaussians $\mathcal{G}_{canon}$ is defined in a canonical coordinate system, storing base parameters: mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, rotation $\mathbf{q}_i \in \mathbb{R}^4$ (unit quaternion), scale $\mathbf{s}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, opacity $\sigma_i$, and spherical harmonics coefficients $\mathbf{c}_{SH,i}$ . For a given time $t$, a deformation function $D$ predicts offsets $(\delta\boldsymbol{\mu}, \delta\mathbf{q}, \delta\mathbf{s})$ based on the canonical position and time . The time-varying parameters are computed as:
$$ \boldsymbol{\mu}_i(t) = \boldsymbol{\mu}_i + \delta\boldsymbol{\mu} $$
$$ \mathbf{s}_i(t) = \mathbf{s}_i + \delta\mathbf{s} $$
$$ \mathbf{q}_i(t) = \text{Normalize}(\mathbf{q}_i \otimes \delta\mathbf{q}) $$
where $\otimes$ is quaternion multiplication and normalization prevents drift [G]. The deformation network $D$ typically takes spatial embeddings of canonical positions and temporal embeddings of time $t$ as input . Rendering uses standard differentiable rasterization with the updated Gaussians, camera pose, and time $t$ [G]. Optimization minimizes photometric loss $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{rec} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{reg}$, updating Gaussian parameters and network weights via SGD .

### Drive-GS
Drive-GS is a variant designed for end-to-end driving simulators [S1, unofficial]. It adapts the deformation framework to support autonomous driving scenarios, likely integrating sensor models for camera and LiDAR realism within the dynamic scene representation [S1, unofficial].

### 4D-Driving-GS
4D-Driving-GS is a method that drives time-of-day and weather conditioning for closed-loop simulation [S1, unofficial]. It extends the deformation model to handle environmental variations over time, enabling realistic rendering of dynamic scenes under changing atmospheric conditions for autonomous vehicle testing [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The family originates from the extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting [G] to dynamic scenes, addressing the limitations of static representations in video data. The dominant pattern for autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation in 2026 involves per-actor 3DGS plus per-scene 3DGS background, forming the basis for internal closed-loop simulators at companies like Tesla, Waymo, and Wayve [S1, unofficial]. Variants like Drive-GS and 4D-Driving-GS specifically target the needs of end-to-end driving simulators and closed-loop simulation with environmental conditioning [S1, unofficial].
